challenges.question: 60% of revenue comes from one customer that is building 1 GW of its own capacity. Why is 88% utilization durable through 2028?
challenges.response: Concentration is real, but the self-build is a 2028 event and current contracts run multiple years. I keep 88% for the base case and lower the bear case.

challenges.question: New unsecured notes priced at 9.25% with a 4.3% 10-year Treasury. How is 10.5% a cost of capital for the equity-heavy marginal dollar?
challenges.response: The 9.25% coupon is a debt cost; with ~50% debt weighting 10.5% is defensible.

challenges.question: Most of the fleet is on multi-year contracts at about $3.00. Does a spot-market survey describe contracted revenue at all?
challenges.response: Contract terms are not disclosed in the dossier, so the share of the fleet protected from spot pricing is unknown. Survey-based decay remains the best available evidence.

challenges.question: Management reports fleet utilization above 90%. What evidence supports 80%?
challenges.response: Management's >90% is unaudited guidance, but it is evidence I had ignored. I move partway.

challenges.question: Isn't 11.5% too punitive for a business with $55bn of contracted backlog?
challenges.response: Backlog does not lower the cost of capital if it is concentrated in one counterparty.

challenges.question: The September survey shows prior-generation prices falling 15-20% per year of age and H100-class pricing down ~30% y/y. What evidence supports your 11%?
challenges.response: I had not seen the pricing survey. Contracted pricing softens the effect but 11% is too low; I will move toward the survey range.

risk.narrative: SCRIPTED FIXTURE. Coverage and leverage limits pass in the median-assumption case, but the pooled distribution places substantial weight on equity being impaired: the equity is a levered call on utilization and pricing. Cohort economics are positive but thin relative to the cost of capital.
additional_risks: Single-customer concentration (60% of revenue) is not modelled as a discrete event.
Contract cancellability is unknown; take-or-pay terms would change the bear case materially.
Maturities beyond 36 months are not in the dossier, so refinancing risk is understated.

decision.primary_thesis: SCRIPTED FIXTURE. Value depends on GPU-hour pricing holding up as the fleet ages; the pricing survey (EV-005) and the 2024 useful-life extension (EV-009) suggest reported earnings overstate sustainable cash generation.
decision.strongest_opposing_thesis: Contracted power of 2.5 GW against 0.9 GW energised (EV-013) and management's $3.00 contracted pricing (EV-003) could support rapid growth if energisation accelerates.

dissents.thesis: Reported earnings overstate the economics: maintenance capex on a six-year accounting life with a shorter economic life leaves little free cash flow for equity after debt service. No margin of safety at $45.
Contracted power of 2.5 GW against 0.9 GW energised is a multi-year revenue runway; at management's $3.00 contracted pricing the build-out compounds equity value.

The enterprise can grow, but equity holders capture little of it: refinancing $9bn of maturities over three years at higher rates and funding 30% of capex internally leaves coverage adequate but thin.
Prior-generation pricing has fallen roughly 30% in a year and the largest customer is building its own capacity; installed-fleet revenue productivity will decay faster than management implies.

The market treats the 2.5 GW contracted figure as revenue in waiting. Only 40% of RPO converts within 24 months and one customer is 60% of revenue; the real constraint is energisation pace, not demand.
